House resumed at eight o'clock.

Mr. Speaker, we rarely witness the spectacle we had t]his afternoon in regard to this debate, probably one of the most important debates during the session, the one in which the public will take more interest probably than all others. When the hoii. Minister of Finance (Hon. Mr. Fielding) had delivered his budget speech, when he had settled so far as the expectations of the people were concerned any question that may have arisen in regard to the tariff, when he had generally entered upon a discussion of the finances of the country during the past year, and when an hon. gentleman on this side of the House had risen in his place and replied todlim, we found, for the first time in the parliament of Canada, I will venture to say during the whole history of the parliament of Canada, hon. gentlemen put on that splendid, but ill-concealed disdain and refused to make reply to the hon. gentleman who answered the speech of the hon. Minister of Finance. What have we now V The House is barely graced with the presence of the right hon. Prime Minister (Rt. Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier). There is not another minister of the Crown in his place.
They are in cold storage.

My hon. friend (Mr. Bennett) says that they are in cold storage. 1 hope that they are in some place that will cure them. I shall not enter upon a discussion of a matter that is not the subject fairly of debate, namely, whether we are living to-day in a period of very great expansion, whether we are living in, to use a common phrase, good times. This has not been at all a matter of dispute. It is a proposition to which both sides of the House will assent and I, therefore, am not going' to discuss that phase of the question, nor am I going to discuss the question whether lion, gentlemen opposite have been the authors to any extent of this condition or whether they have been, on the other hand, the means of preventing it. If I should have anything to say in that regard it would be that lion, gentlemen have not made the most of their advantages. Now, Sir, just let me say that there seems to me to be no more critical period in the history of any country than a period of great expansion. What is the effect of great expansion ? The lion. Minister of Finance very aptly said this afternoon : [DOT] We will have periods of depression, but these are periods of recuperation. They are periods for what purpose? There are those periods that must follow periods of great expansion for the purpose of catching up. In other words, we have been discounting the future and I am not disposed to take that rosy view of it that the lion. Minister of Finance took when he was asked if he expected the present state of things to continue and if he would go on with the same expenditures and the same taxation. The answer of the hon. gentleman was that he did propose to go on with the same expenditures and the same taxation. 1 think the hon. gentleman has given a distinct note of warning to the country that he will take no notice of that state of things, to use a very happy phrase of his own ' when the pendulum swings the other way.' No one can doubt the fact that we will have after this expansion a period of depression. If that were not the case it would be to set aside the rule that has so long prevailed in all countries and nobody would attempt to consider whether that would be a recurring incident in Canada as it has been in other countries and as it lias been in Canada. What is the duty of a government during a period of great expansion ? Is it to maintain taxation, is it, professedly under a revenue tariff, to extract large sums from the people and find means of expending them ? We still have a policy of high taxation. When hon. gentlemen opposite had a splendid opportunity to redeem their pledges to the country, when they could have lowered the tariff, when they could have made decreases to a considerable extent in the taxation, wlint did they do ? They, in the face of every pledge made, turned their backs upon these pledges.
47 i
and they are to-day collecting more taxes than ever were collected from the people of Canada. They are boasting of their surplus and they are doing this in the name of a revenue tariff. In 1896, the then Minister of Finance collected from the people under what was said to be a high protective tariff $36,618,000, and in 1900, the present Minister of Finance collected, under a so-called revenue tariff, $51,029,000. I would like to ask the hon. gentleman whether he considers now that he should still maintain the name of a revenue tariff ? The increase, comparing these two years, in the taxation collected amounts to some $14,411,000. The hon. gentleman received a very generous measure of applause this afternoon when lie told the House and the country that he had a surplus of $8,000,000. Hon. gentlemen opposite are on record in this House as to the value of surpluses. Hon. gentlemen, both in and out of this House, set their faces against surpluses and told the people that when you take large sums of money from the people it means that you have taken money out of the people's pockets which should be there. If hon. gentlemen were prepared to say that they had taken less money, that, by economy, or the proper expenditure of money, they had been able to hare a surplus after having fairly met all the proper services of the country, that would be a proper boast to make, but hon. gentlemen have taken the opposite course. It does seem extraordinary that they should be found boasting of their surpluses. I do not see the Minister of Customs (Hon. Mr. Paterson) in his place, but this is what that hon. gentleman had to say.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: He is in North Bruce.

My hon. friend (Mr. Taylor) says that he is in North Bruce. Well, he was here at one time, and in 1883, referring to the surplus, he said :
Sir,-This surplus business is quite understood by the people of this country. If the surplus was paid by the minister himself, if he had some means of taking it out of his own pocket and putting it into the public treasury, or if the combined supporters of the ministry had some means of putting that money into the treasury, then we would hail them as benefactors of their country. But, when the hon. Minister of Finance has put his hand into your pocket, and my pocket, and the pockets of the people of this country, and taken therefrom this $16,000,000, then we claim that he has not accomplished any great feat though backed in his act by the parliament of this country.
I am going to ask the hon. Minister of Finance if that language applies to him. 1 am going to ask him, if one of his colleagues used that language on one occasion, what is his position to-day ? The hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce (Hon. Sir Richard Cartwright) criticised with great ability the finances of this country. That was precisely the position the hon. gentleman took, and if that is the position he took in the

past, I would like to ask the hon. gentleman to explain to-day why he takes precisely the opposite position. Mr. Speaker, lion, gentlemen may ignore the past, they may turn their backs upon their pledges, but the facts remain just as they were in 1883, when this speech was made and afterwards when several speeches were made by the Minister of Trade and Commerce and other hon. gentlemen on that side of the House. I leave hon. gentlemen without further discussion to settle that with their own consciences. Let the public read what hon. gentlemen said in the past under precisely similar circumstances, and let mem observe the conduct of those who are charged with the affairs of the country now. I expected that the Minister of Finance (Hon. Mr. Fielding) would sing the old song and claim credit to his government, that if the good times were not wholly to be attributed to the administration they were at least in great part due to the wisdom of himself and his colleagues. It is just as well that I should call the attention of the House to this phase of the question, so that the government may know something about their past record on this matter. In 1883, there was a period of phenomenal expansion in trade following one of great depression, and this is what the Minister of Customs then said in regard to the condition of the country :
The Minister of Finance did not raise the price of cheese or butter in Liverpool. That is a matter outside and beyond him. That is the work of the grand eternal law of nature and the law of supply and demand. It was due to the scarcity in foreign countries. We had the articles to sell. The price went up, and the result was that the increased wealth was given to us. Then, Sir, take agricultural products, and what do we find? Why, Sir, we find that in the year 1880 we exported of these products $2,000,000 worth, and in the next year we exported $16,000,000 worth, and last year we exported $11,000,000 worth, or in these three years, as a result of the increased sale at higher prices, we brought hack in gold into this country $15,712,000 more than in 1879. Well, Sir, will the hon. gentleman claim, will he dare to say that he was the cause of the rain falling and the sun shining on our fields, that he was the cause of the abundant harvest of 1882. No, Sir, he will not venture to do so. Will he seek to claim that he stands in the room of Providence, and causes the rain to fall in superabundance in England and Ireland and Scotland, rotting the crops, producing a scarcity of them and increasing the price of the articles we have to sell. Sir, he will not dare to say that he was the cause of Providence smiling on us in this land, and by which we are able to show $15,000,000 more of a result.
Does not that language apply precisely to the condition of affairs to-day. The bon. gentlemen opposite were fortunate to come into power on the eve of a great expansion in trade, and to this and not to anything they have done is due whatever prosperity there is in this country. I shall leave that

also to hon. gentlemen opposite to settle amongst themselves.
Now, with regard to the value of this preference to England. The Minister of Finance challenged this side of the House, that if we were not in favour of the preference, that the only course left open to us was to introduce a resolution demanding its repeal. I do not think the hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Fielding) was sincere in that challenge, nor do I think that on reflection he will consider it a fair challenge. What is the position of affairs to-day ? Why these hon. gentlemen opposite have entered into what we have very properly called a one-sided trade relation with Great Britain ; a trade relation that has not a single redeeming feature, as is shown by the experience we have had of it, a trade relation that imposes $2,000,000 more burden on the people on account of the decreased revenue it brings about, and which $2,000,000 must he recouped from some quarter. The government have entered into this trade relation without getting the slightest return from it. I in my turn will challenge any gentleman opposite to point out some specific instance where Canada benefits today by the preference which we give to Great Britain. It is all very well for the hon. gentlemen to make general statements about this, but let us pin them down to laying their hand upon one example from business experience, in which this country benefits, and they cannot do it. They will tell us : Oh, we have gained the sympathy of Great Britain ; we have touched the hearts of the English people and they are yearning to buy our goods. Well, Sir, it does seem to me that such an argument should not emanate from the brains of sensible men. It is only child's talk for public men to make a pretense of that kind. Why, there is not one man in a thousand in Great Britain who knows that their country has a preference in the Canadian market, and there is not one man in a thousand who cares whether she has a preference or not. The buyer in England will buy the most goods he can for the least money, irrespective of where those goods come from, and the buyer in Canada will do the same thing. We have won our way in the English market on the same conditions as we have won our way in the markets of other countries. Our goods must depend upon their superiority in the market over the goods of other countries, and if we have made England and Germany buy our goods, it is because we are able to produce better and cheaper goods than the people of any other country in the world. These gentlemen opposite now tell us that we have touched the sentimental aspect of this question by giving this preference, but as to that we have the evidence of a gentleman who was very profuse in the session of 1897 with regard to how far sentiment went in Great Britain. That hon. gentleman was then quite as cautious and
quite as prudent as his friends are now 1 never to go beyond a statement of glittering generalities with regard to this ques- : tion. Speaking with regard to the tariff of 1879, which was in force in 1883, the Minis- i ter of Customs (Hon. Mr. Paterson) made this statement, and I want this language 1 placed alongside the language that he and his colleagues are using to-day :
Now let me say, if it would be of any comfort to bon. gentlemen, that in this matter I speak entirely for myself, and I do not attach or never did attach as much importance to the question of imports from Great Britain and the United States respectively as some hon. gentlemen have attached to them.
True, 1 recognize the fact that in England we borrow our money. That her flag floats over us. That her army and navy are pledged to defend us, and therefore it was not exactly the thing that might be called very loyal to Great Britain to put on a tariff that would legislate especially against her. X have gone that far in sentiment, but we all know that in matters of trade there is very little sentiment.
Was that the opinion of hon. gentlemen opposite then ? I would venture to say that every one of them took precisely the same view, and I am bound to say that it was a rational and sensible view-a view which all men would take to-day, if they were not enslaved to circumstances of political advantage.
But we are told that by reason of the preference the people of Canada get cheaper goods. We have been told in the past, and I should not be surprised if we are told again, that by reason of the preference goods coming from other countries than Great Britain are, of necessity, correspondingly reduced in price. That is a broad statement, and demands some examination. Let us take the country to the south of us. Hon. gentlemen who have given any attention to the matter know that there are two distinct fields of operation for the trade of tne United States and the trade of Great Britain. True, there is a common ground on which they met, but it is a small ground. There is a large ground in which the imports from the United States and other countries do not come into competition with the imports from Great Britain. But suppose they did. will any hon. gentleman go so far as to assert that if a gentleman from New York went to purchase a certain kind of goods in London or Manchester, he would have to pay anv more for them than a gentleman from Montreal ? If hon. gentlemen are not prepared to take that ground, then it seems to me they are without any sensible foundation for claiming any advantage for Canada in that respect. Take the case of the United States and Canada. We know that the United States to-day are manufacturing very largely in almost every line of goods that England has to sell. Of course, sometimes a single line of goods not made to any extent in the United States, or a higher grade
of goods, are sometimes purchased in Great Britain, while of other grades of the same goods we buy very large quantities in the United States. For instance, would any hon. gentleman say that where a man buys broadcloth and another buys tweeds, the broadcloth comes into competition with the tweeds ? It is absolute folly, it seems to me, for any hon. gentleman to take a position of that kind.
The Minister of Finance stated this afternoon that we cannot hope to get a preference by huckstering or by demanding a preference, or without England being convinced that it is in her interest to give us a preference. What is the position of the two parties on this matter V One party has given a one-sided preference without any compensation whatever. The other party has demanded, and if it had continued in power and had the control of this country, it would have entered upon a preference, if a preference at all was entered upon, that would have had two sides, and would have commended itself to both countries entering into the contract. Are we to get a preference by hon. gentlemen declaring that it would be madness on the part of England to give us a preference ? Are we to get a preference when we have hon. gentlemen supporting the government declaring that it would be a piece of impudence on the part of Canada to ask a preference ? Read what a gentleman who stands high in the councils of that party has said on the question. The hon. member for North Norfolk (Mr. Charlton)- I am sorry he is not in his place to-nightspeaking on this question last session, and referring to the limited trade Canada had with Great Britain, said :
This is a very small trade relatively, less than 2i per cent of her exports to the world, only one mill In excess of 3h per cent of her exports to foreign countries, 6 8-10 per cent of her exports to British possessions, and yet, we stand up with this comparatively insignificant portion of British trade, and with sublime impudence, ask England to tax herself for the benefit of this little Oliver Twist that is continually calling for more.
Now, I would like to ask how we are to got a preferential trade with Great Britain ? Are we going to get it when we have hon. gentlemen on that side of the House prompted to get up in their places and make statements of that kind ? But the hon. gentleman went further. He said :
If it can be shown, as it can undoubtedly be shown clearly, that the adoption of the policy the hon. gentleman asks for, would impair the prosperity and strength of Great Britain, why, we would be asking, even if we could obtain it, something actually not in our own interest.
The hon. member for North Norfolk not only declared that it was madness to talk of a : preference, but that it was not in the inter, est of Canada to have such a preference.
Well, I believe we are entering upon a peri iod when the statesmen of England must

educate the people of Great Britain in regard to the completely changed circumstances of to-day. The people of that country may be slow to take notice of the rapid changes which are occurring ; but the British manufacturers are becoming justly alarmed at the prospect of the American people driving them out of their own market. We have today an instance of that in the fact that Great Britain, which formerly did nearly all the iron trade of this country, has to-day less than C per cent of it. It is an alarming state of things. There never was a period when there was a better opportunity for the people of Canada and the statesmen of Great Britain to prepare for the changed circumstances, and to realize that nothing short of a trade preference between Great Britain and her colonies can protect the mother country against the evils arising to-day from foreign competition.
But we had another evidence from the hon. member for North Norfolk (Mr. Charlton). He declared in this House, I think upon the same occasion, that we dared not have a preference in England because if Canada obtained preference in Great Britain, we should invite the hostility of her neighbours to the south. Here is what the hon. gentleman had to say :
Her relations with other commercial powers are of such a character that the introduction of such a policy would be fatal to her interests. It would invite retaliation. It would not only invite it. but it would secure retaliation. England would invite disaster that would surely fall upon her if this unreasonable demand were granted to a country which takes but 5 per cent of her exports and sends but 3J per cent of her imports.
In other words Canada sends so small a quantity of exports to Great Britain and purchases so small a quantity of goods from Great Britain, that we dared not enter upon trade preference with each other lest we invite the hostility of the American people. The hon. gentleman, in order to make his case stronger, depicted what he conceived to be the state of feeling in the United States :
We have seen something of the result in the United States. The members of the joint high commission met at every turn that feeling of animosity which exists in the United States in consequence of the adoption of preferential duties of 121 per cent, to be increased to 25 per cent.
Thus the hon. gentleman argues that we dare not enter into closer trade relations with the mother country because, in the first place, that would prevent all possibility of reciprocity with the United States, and in the second place invite commercial hostility that would be dangerous to Great Britain.
We, however, do not propose to be deterred from the policy we deemed essential to the interests of both Canada and the

mother country by these timid imaginings of the hon. gentleman. We propose to call the attention of the people of Great Britain
to the advantages that will flow from closer connections in trade matters, and particularly to the fact that a duty imposed by the mother, country upon the products of foreign countries would not necessarily advance the price to the English consumer. If Canada were admitted to the markets of Great Britain on specially favoured terms, and if foreign products desired to compete against ours, they would have to be sold at the same prices, and consequently the English consumer would not have to pay a farthing more than he otherwise would.
We have been told that the trade with Great Britain has immensely increased under the policy of the present government. Well, I think it will be admitted that the trade with foreign countries from 1898 to 1900 will be a fair index of the accuracy of the hon. gentleman's statement. It would be well, in view of the statement made by the hon. Finance Minister this afternoon,' showing the increase by years in trade with Great Britain, that he should give us the corresponding years with
tlie United States. When asked for that information, he replied that he did not have a statement of the trade with the United States during that period.
Let us now compare our trade with the two great trading countries. Great Britain and the United States, in the two periods. First take the exports. The exports to Great Britain increased by a larger percentage than those to the United States. The increase in our exports to Great Britain in 1900, as compared with 1890, was 61 54 per cent, while the increase of our exports to the United States in the same period was 54 34 per cent. On the other hand, our imports from Great Britain increased, in the period I have named, 35 -80 per cent, while our imports from the United States in reased no less than 87 53 per cent. Now, let me compare the aggregate trade with these two countries. Our aggregate trade with Great Britain increased 53 3 per cent, while our aggregate trade with the United States-no inducement offered, no preference given-increased 73-22 per cent. The Finance Minister or hou. genlemen on his side can hardly answer that by merely saying we bought the goods we needed. That was perfectly true, but it only shows that trade will seek the channels of least resistance, and that to the extent that trade goes on each country produces goods that are required by the other. This is further exemplified by the fact that notwithstanding hostile tariffs, our trade with Belgium and Germany has increased by a greater percentage than has our trade with Great Britain.
Now, I shall not detain the House long, but I wish to make some reference to what I consider a very important statement made by the Minister of Finance. I notice that the hon. gentleman had one way of making his calculations up to the present year and another way of making them this year. In making a comparison as to the rate of taxation, he, very fairly, excluded Indian corn, which was imported into Canada and re-exported, for although, appearing in the returns as entered for consumption in Canada, it was well known that this corn was not for Canadian consumption and should not be included. He also excluded coin and bullion, which is usually done in making these calculations. But, perhaps some hon. gentleman on that side can explain why the hon. gentleman excluded coin and bullion in former years and included coin and bullion to-day. In making his comparison this year he includes coin and bullion for all the years covered by his comparison. And why does he do so ? Because to do so tells in favour of his own position, for the quantity of coin and bullion imported into Canada in 1900 was larger than in any previous year, and the effect of including them is to show a reduced percentage of taxation. I do not find fault with the hon. gentleman's previous basis of calculation, and in making up the figures I have followed up the
course which he previously thought the correct one, and have excluded coin and bullion as well as Indian corn, which ought to be excluded, as it merely passed through the country and was not consumed there. I ask your attention to a comparison of the rates of taxation on this basis for the two periods from 1893 to 1896, under Conservative rule, and from 1897 to 1900, under Liberal rule. Take the first period first. In this case, I exclude coin and bullion, but include Indian corn, because under the former tariff corn for consumption was so entered. Thus we see that there has been a reduction in the duties of just 35-100 of 1 per cent in the period of Liberal rule as compared with those under Conservative rule. This is the immense reduction of which the hon. gentleman boasts. And what would this reduction mean in money ? In round numbers it means $1,800,000. And this is the net result of this preference modification of the national policy as adopted by hon. gentlemen opposite. We never contended that there were no faults in the national policy. Like every tariff, it had its objections, but in the case of the national policy as adopted and carried into effect by the Conservatives, those objections were merely minor ones. While in the main it was a wise policy-the fact that it built up Canada being proof of it. And when hon. gentlemen came into office they pretended to modify it. When he announced his first tariff the Minister of Finance stated in most explicit terms that it would not lower taxation, but he had a special tariff that would lower taxation-the preferential tariff. And this is the effect of that lowering of the tariff- 35-100 of 1 per cent. It is not to be wondered at that the effect of the preferential tariff was so small when we consider that less than 26 per cent of the dutiable goods imported into Canada come in under the preference. I can scarcely find terms adequate to describe a policy of that kind, that

we have to-day the national policy as it was understood in the past, modified according to what hon. gentlemen have stated, by a preference, and under which we have achieved such meagre results.
But hon. gentlemen have not been slow in increasing the taxation. I say that apart from that reduction, they have largely increased the tax upon the people. They have increased the customs rate from 1896 to 1900. In 1890 the customs was $3.94 per head and the excise 63 cents, or a combined taxation of $4.57 per head. In 1900 the customs rate had increased to $5.37 and the excise to 83 cepts, a total of $6.21, or an increase of $1.04 since 1896 upon every man, woman and child in Canada.. Hon. gentlemen may say, perhaps, that is not strictly accurate, that it is open to the objection the Minister of Trade and Commerce has urged upon more than one occasion, namely, the mode of calculating the increase of population. But the hon. gentleman is not in a position to do more than state that the mode of calculation is not accurate. However, whether accurate or not, it applies to both cases, and one side has absolutely no advantage over the other.
Now, let us see what has been the result of this taxation. Take the increase of taxes made since 1896 on tobacco and cigars. The extra taxation has been $1,313,337. We have also an increase on sugar, notwithstanding the position taken by the Minister of Finance when he stated that he was going to give a free breakfast table, that he was going to reduce the duty on refined sugar from $1.14 per hundred pounds to $1, that he was going to allow the duty to remain as it was before at one-half cent a pound on raw sugar. We have an increase in duties on sugar by reason of the law governing the test under which it is imported, of no less a sum than $737,534 more than it was in 1896 under the existing duties. Then we collect an increased duty on rice, another article which tlie hon. gentleman was going to make cheaper ; we collect an additional $26,205. Now, I want to call attention to two facts. One is that by reason of the operation of the preferential tariff, according to the Trade Returns, there has been a reduction of $1,180,325. What have we in the way of increased taxation on other articles ? Take tobacco, that is a luxury perhaps to some extent. but to a great multitude of poor men in this country it is their greatest luxury ; we have an increased taxation upon that, as I have already stated, to the extent of $1,313,000 a year ; in sugar. $737,000 in round numbers ; in rice, $26,000 ; in other words, as against a reduction of $1,180,000. we have an increase of $2,077,466. Surely that is not a very comfortable outlook.
Now, I challenge hon. gentlemen opposite to say that we are not paying, under the proposed reduction of hon. gentlemen made on sugar in 1897, nearly three-quarters of a million dollars more in duties than we paid

in 1896. Then the Minister of Finance stated that we imported goods from the United States because they are raw material. Is sugar not raw material ? If you import iron goods for the purpose of aiding manufactures in this country, and of lowering the price of iron manufactures to the consumers, which was the reason alleged, what is the difference between lowering the duties on raw material that is composed of iron and on raw material that is composed of rice, or sugar, which are necessaries of life ? There is, to my mind, a most contradictory position taken by the Minister of Finance. In one class of raw material the duty is not to be lowered, and in another class i,t is to be lowered, yet in both cases he says they will be equally cheap to the people. Now, by reason of the arrangement of the test under which sugars will be entered for duty, he has laid down a rule by which he takes from the people nearly three-quarters of a million dollars more than was taken in 1896. But what was his declaration in 1897 V He declared that he was lowering the duties on sugar to the extent of $400,000 annually. Has he done that ? I do not think the hon. gentleman will contend that he has done it. I do not think the hon. gentleman will contend that he has not advanced the duties to the extent of nearly three-quarters of a million dollars over 1896. Then I would like to know where are the grounds for congratulation which the hon. gentleman and bis friends claim to possess.
Now, Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Finance claimed some credit for reducing the public debt and for having a great surplus. The hon. gentleman went so far as to say that it was really a very gratifying thing that there should' be a reduction of the public debt under the circumstances. Now, I desire to call his attention to the circumstances under which he reduced the public debt. Sir, the circumstance is that he has taken $52,000,000 out of the pockets of the people, the largest sum that was ever collected from the people of Canada. Yet he congratulates himself that while he takes $14,000,000 more from the people than was taken in 1896, he glorifies himself for having made a slight reduction in the public debt. He says they have a great surplus of $8,000,000. Let us see now whether the hon. gentleman has a surplus or not. In arriving at his surplus of $8,000,000, the hon. gentleman did not include all the expenditures. Now, it is a mere trick, I will not say it has been confined to one side of the House, but it is a trick upon the public to found the statement of a surplus upon the expenditure under consolidated revenue. Our receipts in 1899 were $51,029,994, our expenditures for the same year were $52,717,466. or a deficit between the two sides of the ledger of $1,687,472.
I am quite aware, Mr. Speaker, when I make that statement, that this is not the first occasion upon which a surplus has been counted in that way. But, I wish to call
the attention of hon. gentlemen to the fact that we collected $51,000,000 in 1900, and that we expended $52,000,000. What is the answer of hon. gentlemen opposite ? They say that a part of this should be charged to capital account. That is not a fair answer. A fair statement is that we spent more money than we collected; that we made the largest collection that was ever made in Canada, that we made the largest expenditure on the other hand, and, instead of having upon the whole transaction, namely, the sums of money that were spent on capital as well as the sums that were chargeable to consolidated revenue, a surplus, we have, in round numbers $1,087,000 of a deficit. I think that is a fair way of putting it, and if hon. gentlemen boast of that kind of thing, 1 do not think there is very much credit due them. If hon. gentlemen were able to say: We have only charged to capital account such items as properly belong to it, we have not unloaded on capital account for the pur, pose of having a surplus they would be able to make a creditable showing. But, hon. gentlemen, as they have done in connection with the Intercolonial Railway, require to charge endless expenditures to capital account in order to show a surplus. The Minister of Railways and Canals (Hon. Mr. Blair) could have a surplus to such an extent as suits his sweet will by adopting that course. He could charge services to capital account which did not properly belong to capital account as was shown in a debate in this House during last session. It was then shown that he had charged to capital account expenditures in connection with services that had never been so charged before. I do not say that the hon. Minister of Finance is doing that, but, if the expenditures on the Intercolonial Railway which were charged to capital account, form part of that surplus of $8,000,000 it shows how much there is to support the claim of such a surplus. The fact is that hon. gentlemen have paid out over $1,500,000 more than they collected, although the sum collected was very large. Ass to the attitude of hon. gentlemen upon this question in the past I shall not dwell. We have had the spectacle of hon. gentlemen going to the people with one set of professions and coming back and acting on an entirely different set. They have proclaimed that they have a revenue tariff and that they are able to collect $51.000.000 with a surplus of $8,000,000 under that tariff. The very thing that hon. gentlemen declared against in the past. Hon. gentlemen went to the country and declared against the national policy, but, what was the attitude of hon. gentlemen in the past. I suppose I may acquit the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce. He was fortunately silent but the right hon. First Minister was not silent in his early history in regard to being a protectionist. He was
a protectionist in the movement which took place in the province of Quebec in 1870, when the national party was formed. The right hon. gentleman was a member of the legislature of Quebec at that time, and he joined in the movement for protection to the industries of Canada. That was the attitude of the right lion, gentleman upon that occasion. Then, I will take the hon. member for North Norfolk (Mr. Charlton). I am sorry he is not here to-night, because he was very pronounced upon the question of protection. This is what the hon. gentleman had to say before the national policy was adopted in 1878 :
I believe that the interests of the nation at large would be promoted by judicial protection.
I believe that the agricultural industries of the Dominion would be promoted by protection and that the manufacturers, being brought to the door of the farmer, would afford a market for a great many articles that would not be saleable if the market were 3,000 miles away. With a home market of this kind established by protection to manufacturers the agriculturists can benefit by producing a rotation of crops.	'
The right hon. First Minister, although not a member of this House at that time
My hon. friend (Mr. Clancy) is mistaken. The Prime Minister was it member of this House in 1876, and he entered the government of Mr. Mackenzie in 1876 or 1877-I forget which.

Mr. CLANCY, Quite so, but before he came into this House, he had in his province in which he was a distinguished member of the legislature, in which he was a prominent and leading mind in what was known ns the national party, said that he favoured protection to Canadian industries. It is a matter of little consequence whether lie was a member of this House in 187(5. or whether he made the statement upon that occasion or prior to that. The point I am endeavouring to make is that the right lion, gentleman at one time in his life did look favourably upon protection to Canadian industries. Now. we will take the hon. Minister of Customs (Hon. Mr. Paterson) who also entertained a view of that kind. He said :
I must admit that I am in favour of a defensive policy. I cannot view with complacency what we see in this country. We live beside a country with a population ten times greater than our own whose industries have been fostered by protection until they are enabled even in some articles in which Great Britain excels, to challenge supremacy with her. While that nation has erected against us and other countries a hostile tariff, we have our hands bound and give them free and unrestricted rights of trade in our market.
There can be no doubt about the tone of

that speech. That speech was made before the tariff was introduced in 1879. Now, I am going to acquit the lion. Minister of Trade and Commerce of having committed himself, so far as he can be traced, to statements of that kind, but the hon. gentleman had it in his desk. The hon. gentleman believed in protection. There is no doubt about that and I challenge the hon. gentleman to say that he did not believe in protection.

I will show the hon. gentleman when he believed in protection. We have the right hon. Prime Minister who is very candid sometimes, and I sun going to call one of the most respectable witnesses in Canada to prove that the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce was favourable to protection. He is a distinguished member to the party to which he belongs, an hon. gentleman who has done great service to his party, and I am bound to admit that the hon. gentleman with his ability could not fail to perform some service to his country whether we quite agree with the attitude he has maintained during his long years of service or not. But, at a public dinner, given to the hon. gentleman on the 10th of May, 1900, in this city, what was said ? We have an hon. gentleman who rose, not late in the evening, I presume, not at that period when men are influenced or moved by the spirit, but at that sober period when men feel quite candid and the right hon. gentleman was extremely candid. He was referring to the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce when he said :
There never was a day of the many days since we had to discuss questions together in council but I could count and rely on the support of Sir Richard Cartwright; and though, as sometimes happens in the councils of the party, we did not agree when in council, when the policy of the party was agreed upon, Sir Richard Cartwright never wavered in his support of it. I will give you an instance which has come to me from reliable sources, and is a thing which goes far to show the character of the guest of the evening.
Mark the words, Mr. Speaker : the 'character ' of the guest of the evening. I want the Minister of Trade and Commerce. (Hon. 'Sir Richard Cartwright) to note what follows ;
In the days of Mr. Mackenzie, when the country was very much depressed, there were many who believed that if the tariff was increased, that policy would be justified by the necessities of the revenue, and that it would be a valuable policy for the country at large. I can give you the story without betraying secrets, because these things happened before my day, but if the advice of Sir Richard Cartwright had prevailed at that time this policy would have been adopted.
That is the time when the hon. gentleman (Hon. Sir Richard Cartwright) had it in his heart. There is more :

If it was not accepted, it was on account of other influences which prevailed with the government of the day, and for sixteen or twenty years Sir Richard Cartwright bore the brunt of the obloquy of not having responded to public sentiment, whereas the truth was that he was ready to respond to public sentiment. For eighteen years he bore the brunt of all the obloquy and never whispered a word. It is not every day you can find such abnegation and such loyalty to the party, and I have reasons to believe and to repeat it to you, I not only repeat it to you my colleagues, but wish my words to be heard all over Canada, that Canada little knows the debt of gratitude it owes to Sir Richard Cartwright.
Now, Mr. Speaker, by a very easy translation, wbat does this mean ? It means that in 1878, when the Liberal party went to the country, when the hon. gentleman cried out against protection himself, that he had it in his heart and was a believer in protection.

By no manner of means. I have no objection to tell the hon. gentleman (Mr. Clancy). what happened, if he will permit me. For revenue purposes, and for revenue purposes alone, I advised in 1876-the thing is public property-I advised, as is perfectly well known on both sides of the House, an increase of the taxation to about 20 per cent, but it had nothing in the world to do with the question of protection. It was done because there was a deficit or impending deficit. It was done for revenue purposes.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE (Hon. Sir Richard Cartwright).

speechtext: If that be so, the hon. gentleman (Hon. Sir Richard Cartwright) has done his leader manifest injustice. Did the First Minister state the truth or was he doing the Minister of Trade and Commerce ar. injustice ? Why, Sir, the very position that was taken afterwards by the hon. gentleman (Hon. Sir Richard Cartwright) shows it. When his colleagues knew that 'he wanted and believed in protective tariffs-to use plain English as it is understood in Canada
Not protective tariff ; revenue tariff.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext:
The hon. gentleman and his leader will have to settle the question of ' revenue ' and ' protection ' between themselves. The First Minister has put himself on record on that question, and the country will believe the First Minister. The hon. gentleman (Sir Richard Cartwright) who was known to his colleagues to have favoured at least a considerable amount of protection, put himself on record in 1890. I want to show the position of that hon. gentleman (Sir Richard Cartwright) at the two periods in order to see how he stands before the world. He said in 1890 :
I say our protective system was a huge mistake, in so far as it was honest at all, and
in so far as it was not honest, it was a huge scheme of robbery. A small ring clique of combines and protected manufacturers have, as I have told you, been permitted for years to make a prize and plunder of the people of Canada. I stand by the declaration I have made that protection is nothing more or less than deliberate legalized and organized robbery, and more than that, if you do not stamp it out, it is the very high road to political slavery first, and industrial slavery afterwards. Our policy from first to last has been to destroy the villainous system of protection by free trade. Revenue tariff or continental free trade.
That is the position the hon. gentleman occupied during these whole years, when he did what ? When, to use the words of the right hon. the Prime Minister, he bore the brunt of obloquy for not responding to public opinion, and when he bore it in silence and did not dare to act upon the dictates of his own conscience. And what happened ? Notwithstanding that the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir Richard Cartwright) went to his own constituency before the elections of 1896 and declared that if his party were returned to power he would be Finance Minister ; notwithstanding that, he is sentenced to sit at the feet of the present Finance Minister (Hon. Mr. Fielding). And why was that done ? It was done for the reason that was disclosed in the First Minister's speech, who in the most extraordiaary manner at a public dinner felt constrained to disclose the sad picture of Sir Richard Cartwright for eighteen or twenty years bearing in silence the brunt of obloquy because he did not respond to public opinion, I shall not dwell on that further ; I shall leave it for the public to pronounce judgment upon it. We have here to-day a set of gentlemen in office who have gone back on every profession they have made. The hon. member for North Norfolk (Mr. Charlton) laid down the political moral code of hon. gentlemen opposite before the elections of 1890. Speaking at Bracebridge for the Liberal leaders, and hoping at that time to be a minister himself, he used the language which I shall quote. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Charlton) too, has been set aside, and I am not sure that he is not having his revenge in some quarters, X am not sure that he is not giving evidence to the people of Canada that he is not quite pleased with the treatment he received. Mr. Charlton said at Bracebridge :
In concluding his speech he told the audience what the Liberal party will do when they get into office. We will stop going into debt.
Well, the government have not done that. Why, Sir, we have had a declaration even this afternoon from the Finance Minister that, notwithstanding they claim a surplus of $8,000,000 ; we had the declaration from the Finance Minister this afternoon that the government claimed a surplus of $8,000,000 odd ; the revenue collected from the
people in the form of taxation is said to be $52,000,000 in the present year; and we have the announcement from the Finance Minister that, notwithstanding that fact, he proposes to run into debt during the present year to the amount of nearly $2,000,000. This is what the hon. member for North Norfolk said on that occasion :
We will stop going into debt. We will adopt principles ot honesty and economy.
Leaving aside the very difficult and irritating question as to honesty, where is the economy ?
We will out down the annual expenditures by four or five millions of dollars. We will bring about prosperity to the farmers by promoting reciprocal trade relations with their natural market.
Namely, that of the United States. Has that been done ? And lastly :
We will have the same code for public as for private morals.
It is fair to say, Mr. Speaker, that that was too refined altogether for the hon. gentlemen. No wonder my hon. friend said that a gentleman committing a party to a position of that kind, should be consigned to the place he holds to-day.
I say we can well afford to leave this matter to the judgment of public opinion. We have hon. gentlemen here to-day occupying a position just the opposite of that which they occupied before. We have hon. gentlemen declaring that wTe have no protection, when we have a protective tariff. With regard to our position on the question of the one-sided preference and the challenge the Finance Minister made this afternoon on the subject of the preference, I am speaking for myself entirely when I say that it is not the business of the Conservative party to repeal a one-sided, silly and senseless preference which hon. gentlemen opposite adopt ; but it is the business of the Conservative party to undo by all rational means the mistakes and misdeeds of hon. gentlemen opposite. The policy of the Conservative party is to educate our own people and the people of Great Britain too ; because I think the speeches made in this House are not without effect on public sentiment in Great Britain. We have gentlemen in this House capable of pointing out the immense advantages that would inure to the British Empire from trade relations carried on within the empire, as against every other country in the world. Is that not a reasonable and rational proposition which will commend itself to public sentiment in Great Britain ? We must help to educate the people of Great Britain to see the advantage of a condition of things that would be of mutual benefit to the people of Great Britain and to the people of Canada. But I despair, as the people of this country have reason to despair, of the consummation of

that great achievement for Canada and the empire-and it will be a great achievement when it is brought about, as I hope it will be in the near future-so long as we have hon. gentlemen on that side of the House declaring that the people of Great Britain would be madmen and fools if they assented to anything of the sort.
This is, in short, the difference between the two parties on this question. We believe that this country has a great future as a part of the British Empire; but we believe it has a future and destiny of its own that warrants it in having a fiscal policy of its own. We believe we are not called upon to go to another country and say, We will give you this for the pleasure of taxing people who are already impoverished by taxation. I challenge hon. gentlemen opposite to lay their finger on a single feature that can be urged on behalf of the present preference. What were the declarations made by the Liberal party in 1896 and laid down in the platform adopted in their convention in 1893 ? To reduce taxation on the necessaries of life. As the only modifying feature of what is to-day a decidedly protective tariff-and I am not finding fault with it on that ground-we have the preference which covers less (than 26 per cent of all the dutiable goods imported into Canada. In that 26 per cent do the necessaries of life come in on more favourable terms than the luxuries ? No, Sir ; there is that fatal cut which admits all the luxuries of life on the same ground as the most pressing necessaries. Then, I ask hon. gentlemen where are the modifying features of this tariff to show that they carried out their pledge of 1896 to lighten the burden of taxation on the necessaries of life ? I will not say that there are not some cases, but they are so trivial and unimportant that they amount to nothing in the way of reducing the taxation. Now, I repeat that while our attachment to Great Britain needs not the proof of this one-sided policy, the people of this country have shown, when the occasion has arisen, that they need give no such proof of their loyalty to the mother country. There are no dollars and cents in it. If we had to prove our loyalty to the mother country by concessions on the basis of dollars and cents, that would be the lowest ground on which we could put it. I repeat, that while we have an interest and a destiny which is inseparable from Great Britain and which we do not desire to have separated, we have a future of our own ; and I believe that the best way we can serve the interests of the empire is by making our own country great and prosperous.

Mr. Speaker, it is not my purpose to inflict .a fourth financial speech on the House to-Mr. CLANCY.
night. Three are, I think, as much as the average digestion of ordinary members of parliament can very well endure ; and, therefore, with the assent of hon. gentlemen, I would move the adjournment of the debate.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE (Hon. Sir Richard Cartwright).

speechtext: Might I ask when it is proposed to resume the debate-to-morrow or Monday ?
To-morrow.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: Will it proceed from day to day ?
We shall be glad to consult the convenience of hon. gentlemen on that point.

Motion agreed to, and debate adjourned.
On motion of the Prime Minister, House adjourned at 9.30 p.m.
Friday, March 15, 1901.
